newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 7.

text.p: THE DOMINION

United States President Bill Clinton won a sweeping re-election victory on Tuesday, but his Democrats failed to recapture congress from the Republicans, guaranteeing a divided government to continue the fierce partisan battles of the past two years. Page 1.

A new legal requirement for companies to reveal top executives' salaries has yet to affect Air New Zealand. The airline refused to reveal at its annual meeting on Wednesday what it was paying managing director and chief executive Jim
McCrea, saying it did not have to comply till next year. Page 1.

The diplomatic protection squad on Wednesday night retrieved the lost briefcase of prime ministerial press secretary Richard Griffin from a Wellington hotel. Griffin said there were no papers in the case relating to coalition talks. Page 1.

NZ First leader Winston Peters on Wednesday indicated the timetable for coalition talks could be lengthening, saying it was difficult to forecast how long negotiations would last. Speaking after talks with National, Peters said his party would
continue negotiating with both National and Labour before narrowing the talks down to one party. Page 2.

Chinese Premier Li Peng paid a brief unofficial visit to New Zealand on Wednesday and held discussions with Foreign Minister Don McKinnon before flying to South America. A spokeswoman for McKinnon described their 15-minute meeting as a "light discussion" covering a range of issues including human rights, trade and the forthcoming meeting of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Page 2.

Details of interim funding allocations would be given to tertiary institutions on Thursday, Education Minister Wyatt Creech said. Creech, who had been under mounting pressure to make the information public, had argued that as a caretaker minister he was unable to issue it. On Wednesday, NZ First leader Winston Peters, university staff and students said the 1997 allocations should be made known as soon as possible. Page 2.

State-house tenants hoping for a reprieve from planned rent increases will be pinning their hopes on the outcome of informal talks between NZ First and National about a possible rent freeze. NZ First leader Winston Peters said after coalition talks with National on Wednesday that a bipartisan "subcommittee" was being set up to discuss state-house rent increases, due to take effect from this month. Page 2.

New Zealanders could have up to 100 television channels to choose from by the end of next year, a television executive said on Wednesday. Mike O'Sullivan, chief executive of marketing advisory company Channel i, said the media revolution would affect every marketing company and every industry. Page 3.

A six-year high in fuel prices would force Air New Zealand to raise its air fares to recover costs if they continued in 1997, company chairman Bob Matthew told the annual meeting in Auckland on Wednesday. Though Air New Zealand expected to post a result below the $225 million profit reported for the year to
June, Matthew said there were inititatives being taken "in difficult times", such as Project Save. The company expects to cut $100 million annually in operating costs through the programme. Page 14.

Inflationary risks still exist, Reserve Bank governor Don Brash says in the bank's annual report, made public on Wednesday. Dr Brash says the past year was "challenging", with the breach of the 0-2 percent inflation target "highly undesirable". Brash said housing market pressures seemed to be abating, but it would be a mistake to assume that all problems
with inflation pressures were solved once house prices stabilised or fell. Page 14.
Appliance manufacturer and technology group Fisher and Paykel made a $19.2 million bottom-line profit for the six months to September 30. Page 14.

Exports of food and beverages increased 7.1 percent to reach a record $9.63 billion in the year to September 30, but profit in the food industry could be improved, the Food and Beverage Exporters Council said. Page 14.

ECNZ on Wednesday denied water was being spilled from hydro dams in the South Island while more expensive thermal stations were operating in the North Island. The Major Electricity Users Group this week suggested thermal energy could be displacing hydro power. Page 14.

Heinz Wattie subsidiary Tip Top Ice Cream has a conditional agreement with Dairy Group subsidiary United Dairy Foods to buy its New American novelty, family pack, and scoop icecream business. Page 14.

The troubled Golden Cross mine near Waihi suffered a significant fall in gold output in the three months to the end of September, while production costs have rocketed. Financial results from Coeur d'Alene Mines, which owns 80 percent of Golden Cross, show the mine produced 16,317 ounces of gold in the quarter, 29 percent down on the amount produced in the quarter last year. Page 15.

Kiwi Income Property Trust unit holdings on Wednesday approved the issue of 60.45 million convertible notes to finance the purchase of a parcel of commercial properties in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch sold by Sentry Investments for $91.5 million. Page 15.

A last-minute flurry this week encouraged Dublin-based Independent Newspapers to extend its takeover bid for Wilson and Horton by a week, to November 15. At close of trade on Wednesday night INP had lifted its stake to just under 73 percent of Wilson and Horton. Page 15.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD
While United States President Bill Clinton won a sweeping victory on Wednesday, his Democrats' failure to take Congress from the Republicans has guaranteed a divided government.

The nation's chief inflation fighter, Reserve Bank governor Don Brash need have no worries about his own personal money supply. For keeping watch over our economic destiny, Brash is thought to pick up some $360,000 a year. That is nearly twice the Prime Minister's pay. On the other hand, it is not even a
third of the salary Rod Deane gets for running Telecom.

Labour believes NZ First should declare a preference by the end of this month. Labour leader Helen Clark said on Wednesday the new Government needed time to prepare the Speech from the Throne. This is read by the Queen and is used to outline to Parliament the Government's legislative agenda.

Nigeria has finally offered what seems to be a satisfactory invitation for a fact-finding mission - which will include the New Zealand foreign minister - to visit the oil-rich West African country suspended from the Commonwealth last year.

Crown Health Enterprises caretaker minister Bill English has backed a call by an Auckland health chief to stop bailing out "sloppy" hospitals. Other hospital bosses have labelled the call simplistic, generalised and narrow minded.

Air New Zealand is close to tying up alliances with some of its international competitors, the airline's annual meeting in Auckland heard on Wednesday. Chairman Bob Matthew told shareholders they could expect "major financial benefits" from the deals, although it would be six months or so before any earnings impacts started to be felt. He said it would be premature to say anything further. But Singapore Airlines has been tipped as a codeshare partner for Air New Zealand.

News of three-year Eurokiwi bond issue in the name of Walt Disney gave the kiwi a solid start, boosting its value to a high of US 71.15 cents from the US71.06 cents open. Then Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith said the kiwi had gone above where economic strength suggested it should be. That sent the kiwi to a low of 70.89 cents before it recovered to finish at 71 cents.
